section.title: Calculating limits
section.p: A table can point toward a limit, but a table only checks a few inputs. A graph can reveal the shape, but a graph depends on the viewing window. Algebra lets us prove what the nearby values are doing.
The first limits we can calculate are the ones where nearby behavior is preserved by arithmetic.

subsection.title: A first limit law from an example
subsection.p: Suppose f(x)=x^2 and g(x)=3x-1. As x\to 2, f(x)\to 4 and g(x)\to 5.
Now look at their sum: f(x)+g(x)=x^2+3x-1. As x\to 2, this approaches 4+5=9, so
The limit of the sum is the sum of the limits. The same thing happens for products: f(x)g(x)=x^2(3x-1)\to 4\cdot 5=20 as x\to 2.
The nearby behavior of the pieces controls the nearby behavior of the expression built from them.

paragraphs.title: Why the sum law is believable
paragraphs.p: If f(x) is close to L, and g(x) is close to M, then f(x)+g(x) should be close to L+M. The error is controlled by the triangle inequality:
If both errors on the right are small, the total error is small.

warning.title: Quotient law needs nonzero limiting denominator
warning.p: Consider \frac{1}{x} as x\to 0. The denominator approaches 0, and the quotient does not approach a finite number. We cannot use the quotient law when the denominator's limit is 0.

warning.title: Limit laws do not work backward
warning.p: It is possible for a sum to have a limit even when the individual pieces do not. For example, for x\neq 0, let f(x)=\sin\frac{1}{x} and g(x)=-\sin\frac{1}{x}. Neither piece has a limit as x\to 0, but f(x)+g(x)=0, so \lim_{x\to 0}(f(x)+g(x))=0.

subsection.title: Polynomials and direct substitution
subsection.p: A polynomial is built from constants, powers of x, sums, and products. Since \lim_{x\to a}x=a, repeated products give \lim_{x\to a}x^n=a^n for positive integers n.

subsection.title: Rational functions
subsection.p: A rational function is a quotient of polynomials: R(x)=\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}. If the denominator is not approaching 0, the quotient law applies directly.

subsection.title: When cancellation does not save the limit
subsection.p: Not every \frac{0}{0} expression has a removable hole. Consider \frac{x}{x^2}. For x\neq 0, \frac{x}{x^2}=\frac{1}{x}. As x\to 0, this does not approach a finite number. So \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{x^2} does not exist as a finite limit.

statement.p: The symbol \frac{0}{0} is called an indeterminate form. It means the expression needs more algebraic work and does not determine the limit by itself.

subsection.title: The squeeze idea
subsection.p: Some limits cannot be found by simplifying an expression into something calm. Instead, we trap the function between two simpler functions.

statement.p: Consider f(x)=x^2\sin\frac{1}{x} for x\neq 0. The factor \sin(1/x) oscillates rapidly as x\to 0, but is always bounded: -1\le \sin\frac{1}{x}\le 1.
As x\to 0, -x^2\to 0 and x^2\to 0. By the Squeeze Principle, \lim_{x\to 0}x^2\sin\frac{1}{x}=0.

subsection.title: A short guide to the first limit tools

row.cell: Use polynomial or rational function rules.
Factor, cancel, expand, or rationalize. Then retry.

Left and right behavior look different
Do not force a two-sided limit; check one-sided limits.
A finite limit does not exist (infinite limit behavior).

subsection.p: These tools are enough for many early limits. Limits can fail from a jump, explode toward infinity, or behave differently on the two sides of a point. The next section separates those possibilities.
